item.title: San Francisco Hot Pot and Shabu
item.description: Eight San Francisco hot pot and shabu rooms where you cook dinner yourself and leave prouder than when you walked in. Fog outside, steam inside, the whole
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Hot Pot and Shabu

Eight San Francisco hot pot and shabu rooms where you cook dinner yourself and leave prouder than when you walked in. Fog outside, steam inside, the whole city misted over while your broth goes to work. From Chinatown to Japantown to the far end of the Sunset, here is where locals dip.

Nabe — 1325 9th Ave, San Francisco. Inner Sunset shabu where the broth is the whole personality and the sake list keeps pace. Organic meat, tidy pots, that foggy-avenue warmth the second you slide into a booth. Open Wednesday through Sunday, so plan the craving around it. @nabe.sf

Hotpot Champ — 801 Kearny St, San Francisco. All-you-can-eat on the Chinatown edge, where the beef and lamb roll out on a literal Ferris wheel and nobody judges a third plate. Bring the friends who order like it is a contest. Kitchen runs past midnight on weekends. @hotpot_champ_sf

Dragon Beaux — 5700 Geary Blvd, San Francisco. The Koi Palace family's Outer Richmond room does dim sum by day, then flips to hot pot at night with live seafood, Wagyu, and geoduck that arrives still forming an opinion of you. Reserve ahead, the lines are a Richmond institution. @dragonbeaux

Fiery Hot Pot and Grill — 2333 Irving St, San Francisco. Outer Sunset spot running smokeless hot pot and Korean BBQ on one table, A5 Wagyu on the menu, so your jacket will not smell like dinner tomorrow. All-you-can-eat, come hungry and a little competitive. @fiery_sf

Matsuyama Shabu House — 1726 Buchanan St, San Francisco. Japantown shabu done the quiet, careful way, thin Wagyu swirled through clean broth with an izakaya lean and a Michelin nod. Closed Tuesdays, packed on weekend nights, so book a table before the Japan Center crowd beats you to it. @matsuyamashabuhousesf

IPOT — 1420 Irving St, San Francisco. A bi-level Inner Sunset favorite since 2015, pairing all-you-can-eat hot pot with Korean BBQ on the same table and eighteen house broths to argue over. Grills and pots going at once, so the indecisive friend finally gets a win. Weekends fill fast. @ipot.food

Boiling Hot Pot — 5512 Geary Blvd, San Francisco. A Richmond all-you-can-eat where you tap four broths into one pot on an iPad and race a ninety-minute clock. Efficient, generous, priced like the neighbors want you back next week. Come early on a Friday, word got out a while ago.

Nan Hot Pot SF — 501 Broadway, San Francisco. Sichuan hot pot on the North Beach and Chinatown seam, mala broth with a numbing kick and a tidy ingredient list that respects a smaller table. Good for two, better for a booth of four after a night out on Broadway. @nanhotpotsf

Eight for steam season across San Francisco: shabu in the Sunset, AYCE off Chinatown, banquet hot pot in the Richmond, Japantown Wagyu, smokeless by the beach, mala on Broadway. Which broth gets you first when the fog rolls in?

item.title: San Francisco Soul Food and Southern
item.description: Eight San Francisco soul food, Southern, and Creole kitchens still cooking the real thing, from a Richmond mainstay that opened in 1999 to a Bayview chef c
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Soul Food and Southern

Eight San Francisco soul food, Southern, and Creole kitchens still cooking the real thing, from a Richmond mainstay that opened in 1999 to a Bayview chef chasing a national gumbo. Everybody names the same couple of spots and misses the rest. Here they are, in the order you should eat your way through them.

Brenda's French Soul Food — 652 Polk Street, San Francisco. New Orleans by way of the Tenderloin, and the line out front is doing you a favor by buying you time to choose between the crawfish beignets and the shrimp grits. Get both. Open till 8, and it closes early on Tuesdays. @brendasfrenchsf

Brenda's Meat & Three — 919 Divisadero Street, San Francisco. The bigger sister on Divisadero runs on a Southern diner rule: one meat, three sides, and a long argument with yourself over which three. The heated back patio lets you linger from breakfast into supper. @brendasmeatandthree

Hard Knox Cafe — 2448 Clement Street, San Francisco. Chef Tony Hua opened the first Hard Knox in 1999, and the fried chicken and catfish still land piled past the edge of the plate. Bring an appetite you can be honest about and plan on a box to go. @hardknoxcafe

The Front Porch — 65 29th Street, San Francisco. On the Bernal and Mission line since 2006, this is the fried chicken and waffles you rearrange a night around, with beignets that show up under a snowdrift of powdered sugar and a tart raspberry dip. Dinner most nights, weekend brunch, and a room that fills the minute the doors swing open. @thefrontporchsf

Po'Boys Kitchen — 317 Connecticut Street, San Francisco. A Potrero Hill counter turning out Cajun-Creole plates, jambalaya, and dressed po'boys with a Bay Area lean. Small room, loud flavors, so call ahead if you want catering trays for the office. @poboyskitchen

Gumbo Social — 5176 3rd Street, San Francisco. Chef Dontaye Ball learned his roux from his grandmother, the one he calls The Big G, and now he wants gumbo named America's national dish from a corner of Bayview. Go Wednesday through Saturday and get the bowl with sausage. @gumbosocial

Old Skool Cafe — 1429 Mendell Street, San Francisco. A youth-run, jazz-themed supper club in Bayview where young people cook and serve international soul food while a live band plays nightly. Book a Wednesday through Saturday dinner and stay for the set. @oldskoolcafe

Peaches Patties — 1 Ferry Building, San Francisco. Chef Shani Jones bakes the flaky Jamaican patty the city did not know it was missing, packed with curried beef or callaloo, with jerk plates and rice and peas alongside. Grab one at the Ferry Building kiosk facing the water and eat it out on the pier. @peachespatties

Eight for soul food across San Francisco: Brenda's French Soul Food, Brenda's Meat & Three, Hard Knox, The Front Porch, Po'Boys Kitchen, Gumbo Social, Old Skool Cafe, and Peaches Patties. Which bowl, plate, or patty gets your Sunday first?

item.title: San Francisco South Bay Filipino Restaurants
item.description: Eight South Bay Filipino spots worth the drive, and most sit where you would never think to look. The real kare-kare, crispy pata, and all-day silog live i
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco South Bay Filipino Restaurants

Eight South Bay Filipino spots worth the drive, and most sit where you would never think to look. The real kare-kare, crispy pata, and all-day silog live in Milpitas strip malls, a Sunnyvale side street, and San Jose turo-turo counters, not a polished downtown row. Here is the run, in order.

Kalesa — 1783 N. Milpitas Blvd, Milpitas. Named for the horse-drawn carriage of old Manila, this family kitchen runs the comfort canon straight: kare-kare, crispy pata, sizzling sisig. Come hungry and come as a group, the party trays are sized for a fiesta, not a Tuesday. Closed Tuesdays, so plan around it. @mykalesa

Max's of Manila — 1535 Landess Ave, Milpitas. The Manila fried-chicken institution landed in a plaza that local Filipino families treat as a second dining room. Order the whole fried chicken with the tangy sarsa, add a plate of lumpia, and skip the diet talk for a night. A crowd-pleaser that earned its name over decades. @maxsmilpitas

Ima's Kusina — 1535 Landess Ave Ste 163, Milpitas. Same plaza, a few doors down, and this one leads with heart: ima means mother in Kapampangan, and the kakanin case makes the case. Load up on suman, ube suman, and turon, then pretend you plan to share the box. Homey delicacies and comfort plates under one roof. @imaskusina

Tapsilog Cantina — 1998 Homestead Rd, Santa Clara. Silog is the Filipino breakfast religion: garlic rice, egg, and your pick of meat, served well past noon because mornings are negotiable. The tapa and the longganisa are the moves here, and a vegetarian silog holds its own too. Closed Mondays, breakfast hours that stretch into dinner. @tapsilog_cantina2020

Clarita's Filipino Cuisine — 905 E Duane Ave, Sunnyvale. A small counter-serve room where the steam trays taste like somebody's lola cooked all morning and the owners clock your order by the third visit. Point at the kare-kare, the bistek, the crispy pata, and let them build the plate. Weekday lunch is the sweet spot before the tech crowd files in.

Tindahan Pinoy — 1647 N Capitol Ave, San Jose. Part Filipino grocery, part silog counter out in Berryessa, open early enough to fuel a work morning. The longsilog is the local order, a juicy longganisa over garlic rice, and the dessert case keeps turon, cassava, and bibingka close. Grab pantry staples on the way out. @tpinoy1647

Jam's Kitchen — 2351 McKee Rd Ste A, San Jose. A family-run Alum Rock kitchen plating home-cooked Filipino food the way somebody's mom would, no polish, all comfort. The rotating steam-tray specials reward regulars who ask what came out fresh today. Closed Mondays, a cozy room that fills with neighbors. @jamskitchensanjose

Manila Turo Turo — 3900 Lake Arrowhead Ave, Fremont. Turo-turo means point-point: you scan the cafeteria-style trays, point at what looks good, and walk out full without spending much. Adobo, pinakbet, dinuguan, whatever the kitchen ran that day. Daytime hours, so make it a lunch run.

Eight for a South Bay Filipino crawl: Kalesa, Max's, Ima's Kusina, Tapsilog Cantina, Clarita's, Tindahan Pinoy, Jam's Kitchen, and Manila Turo Turo. Milpitas to Sunnyvale to San Jose to Fremont, no bridge required. Which one is your first stop, the fried chicken or the silog?

item.title: San Francisco South Bay Seafood Restaurants
item.description: Eight South Bay seafood spots worth the drive, and not one is a chain crab bucket. San Jose keeps its best fish quiet, from a downtown room running since 1
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco South Bay Seafood Restaurants

Eight South Bay seafood spots worth the drive, and not one is a chain crab bucket. San Jose keeps its best fish quiet, from a downtown room running since 1985 to strip-mall Cantonese tanks the neighbors guard, with a Milpitas halal kitchen and a Berryessa boil shack in the mix. Skip the freeway crawl to the coast. The good stuff sits closer than you think, and here is where locals go.

Scott's Seafood — 200 S First St Ste 10, San Jose. Downtown's grown-up seafood room since 1985, white tablecloths, a raw bar, and a seafood boil that ignores the calendar. Book it for the anniversary you keep forgetting, or slide in for oysters at Social Hour, 3 to 6. @scottsseafoodsj

EMC Seafood and Raw Bar — 378 Santana Row Ste 1100, San Jose. The uni pasta gets all the Instagram love, but the move is a seafood tower and a full raw bar tucked into Santana Row's shopping bustle. Open Fridays and Saturdays to midnight, so it survives a movie-then-dinner change of plans. @emcseafood

Blue Water Seafood and Crab — 4180 N 1st St Unit 10, San Jose. An East Coast style crab house up in North San Jose, all cracked crab, fish and chips, and oyster shooters with or without the vodka. Open to midnight daily, patio heaters running, and yes, there are burgers for the one friend who fears the sea. @bluewaternorthsj

Dynasty Seafood — 1001 Story Rd, San Jose. Second floor of Grand Century Mall, this is Cantonese banquet seafood done right, live tanks, carts of dim sum, and big round tables built for a loud family Sunday. Go with a crowd so you can order the whole steamed fish and still have room for har gow.

East Lake Chinese Seafood — 2850 Quimby Rd, San Jose. An Evergreen strip-mall room where the seafood comes straight from the tank and weekend dim sum starts at 10:30. No frills, no view, the kind of neighborhood Cantonese kitchen you'd want three blocks from a new place. @eastlakechineseseafood

Darda Seafood — 296 Barber Ct, Milpitas. Halal Chinese seafood with a Northwest China accent, hand-pulled noodles and clay-pot dishes alongside the fish. Tucked in a Milpitas office park where you'd never look. That's exactly why regulars keep the tables full. @dardaseafoodrestaurant

Claw Shack — 1696 Berryessa Rd, San Jose. Viet-Cajun boil in a bag off Berryessa, where you pick your seafood, pick your sauce, pick your heat, then tie on a plastic bib and dig in with both hands. The Shackie's butter over shrimp and garlic noodles is the order. Closed Mondays, cash-friendly, napkins by the fistful. @clawshack

Mariscos Costa Alegre — 855 N 13th St, San Jose. Nayarit style mariscos on the north side, aguachile, ceviche tostadas, and a molcajete of seafood that arrives steaming and dramatic. Casual, cash-friendly, and open for a long lazy weekend lunch. @costaalegresj

Eight for South Bay seafood: Scott's, EMC, Blue Water, Dynasty, East Lake, Darda, Claw Shack, and Costa Alegre. Raw bar to crab house to Cantonese tank to Viet-Cajun boil, all without crossing a bridge. Which one is landing on your Friday list first?

item.title: Bay Area German and Austrian Beer Halls
item.description: Eight Bay Area German and Alpine beer halls where the pretzels are bigger than your forearm and nobody rushes you off the bench. Old-world beer culture run
item.content:encoded:
Bay Area German and Austrian Beer Halls

Eight Bay Area German and Alpine beer halls where the pretzels are bigger than your forearm and nobody rushes you off the bench. Old-world beer culture runs from Hayes Valley to the Oakland waterfront, long communal tables the whole way. Plan the crawl for a cool evening and bring friends. Here is the lineup, one long table at a time.

Suppenkuche — 525 Laguna St, San Francisco. This Hayes Valley anchor has been pouring German drafts at long communal tables since 1993, back when the neighborhood was still transitional. You sit shoulder to shoulder with strangers, order the sausage plate, and leave with new friends whether you planned to or not. Weekends fill fast, so come early. @suppenkuchesf

Schroeder's — 240 Front St, San Francisco. Founded in 1893, this Bavarian beer hall is one of the oldest restaurants in the city, rebuilt on Front Street after the 1906 quake. It went male-only until the 1970s, a detail the current owners like to note over a stein. Grab the communal table in the FiDi and order the schnitzel. A downtown institution worth the walk. @schroederssf

Radhaus — 2 Marina Blvd, San Francisco. Tucked into Fort Mason with a 200 foot ponderosa bar and a clear view of the Golden Gate Bridge, this Alpine beerhall pours world-class bier next to the water. Walkable from the Marina Green, it draws locals and visitors to the same benches. Come for the doppelbock, stay for the sunset over the bridge. @radhaus_sf

Biergarten — 424 Octavia St, San Francisco. Suppenkuche's open-air little sibling one block away, this Hayes Valley courtyard is the move on a sunny afternoon. Order a pretzel with Obatzda and a cold German beer, snag a picnic table, and settle in. Hours shift with the weather since it is all outdoors, so check before you go. Oktoberfest brings an oompah band. @biergarten_sf

Rosamunde Sausage Grill — 2832 Mission St, San Francisco. A German-inspired California biergarten serving the Mission since 1998, this is the local move for currywurst, a rotating wall of craft and German taps, and Tuesday trivia. The space is tight and pub-style, so expect a friendly crowd. Vegan sausages hold their own here too. Cash-and-cold-beer comfort, no fuss. @rosamundesf

Steins — 731 Clement St, San Francisco. Family-owned and women-owned on Clement Street since 2011, this Inner Richmond beer hall runs a dozen European drafts and puts every major match on the big screens. Bavarian benches, flags on the ceiling, and a boot of Hofbrau make it a proper neighborhood hub. Walk-ins always welcome, which the Richmond appreciates. @steins_sf

Speisekammer — 2424 Lincoln Ave, Alameda. Alameda's German anchor since 2002, a Lincoln Avenue room where the schnitzel arrives the size of the plate and the biergarten out back fills the second the sun shows. Order the jaegerschnitzel and a Weihenstephaner, then let the afternoon run long. Regulars treat it like a second dining room, so a weekend reservation saves you a wait. @speisekammer

Brotzeit Lokal — 1000 Embarcadero, Oakland. Bavarian fare on the Oakland waterfront at Brooklyn Basin, where the biergarten looks across the estuary to Alameda and the sunsets do half the work. Come for the pretzel and a liter, stay for weekend games like cornhole and the wiener dog races. Every table here gets a view, a rare thing this side of the bridge. @brotzeitlokal

Eight for the Bay Area beer hall crawl: Suppenkuche, Schroeder's, Radhaus, Biergarten, Rosamunde and Steins in the city, Speisekammer in Alameda and Brotzeit Lokal on the Oakland water. From an 1893 FiDi institution to a waterfront sunset, the long table tradition holds. Which bench are you claiming first?

item.title: San Francisco Gastropubs
item.description: Eight San Francisco gastropubs where the beer list runs as deep as the dinner menu and nobody makes you pick one. From the Haight to North Beach to SoMa, t
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Gastropubs

Eight San Francisco gastropubs where the beer list runs as deep as the dinner menu and nobody makes you pick one. From the Haight to North Beach to SoMa, this is where locals land when the fog rolls in and a good burger and a proper pour both sound right.

The Alembic — 1725 Haight St, San Francisco. Upstairs from the Haight Street chaos, this narrow room pours a whiskey list longer than most lease agreements and plates small bites that punch well above dive-bar weight. The duck confit and a barrel-aged cocktail is the move. Grab a stool at the tin-topped bar before the after-work crowd claims them. @alembicsf

Magnolia Brewing — 1398 Haight St, San Francisco. The neighborhood brewpub came back from the dead in 2024, and the basement tanks are pouring Kalifornia Kolsch and Proving Ground IPA again like nothing happened. House beer, a burger built for two hands, cocktails now too. Corner of Haight and Masonic, kitchen open til 10. Post up. @magnoliahaight

Comstock Saloon — 155 Columbus Ave, San Francisco. The last standing bar of the Barbary Coast, all 1907 mahogany and pressed tin, where the bartenders take their classics as seriously as the kitchen takes its oysters Kirkpatrick. Come for a Martinez and stay for the pork chop. Aim for the back booths, the front fills fast at happy hour. @comstocksaloon

Bartlett Hall — 242 O'Farrell St, San Francisco. A block off Union Square, this cavernous brick brewhouse makes its own beer and pours barrel-aged cocktails, a small miracle in a neighborhood built for tourists and overpriced hotel bars. The wings and a house lager after a day downtown earn their keep. Big groups fit easy, so bring the crew. @bartletthallsf

The Sycamore — 2140 Mission St, San Francisco. Push through to the hidden back patio and you will forget you are on Mission Street at all. Rotating craft drafts, a kitchen slinging solid burgers and vegan plates, trivia Mondays and bingo Wednesdays for the regulars. It is the kind of low-key corner every neighborhood hopes it lands. Go on a sunny afternoon. @sycamorebeer

Southern Pacific Brewing — 620 Treat Ave, San Francisco. A cathedral-sized Mission warehouse with a mezzanine, a dog-friendly patio, house pilsners and IPAs, and a kitchen leaning Cajun. This is your spot when a party of ten needs beer, burgers, and room to breathe, which the Mission rarely offers. Claim the patio before the sun drops. @southernpacificbrewing

The Willows — 1582 Folsom St, San Francisco. A SoMa gastropub with a craft-beer room, a full bar, board games, and a pinball machine or two for when the conversation lags. The kitchen holds its own past midnight, a rare thing in this city. Rotating drafts, cozy back corners, open til 2 most nights. Land here when dinner runs late. @thewillowssf

The Pig and Whistle — 2801 Geary Blvd, San Francisco. A proper British pub on Geary since 1991, pouring ales from around the world with fish and chips, bangers and mash, and shepherd's pie that tastes like it has nothing to prove. Trivia Wednesdays and Sundays, three-dollar happy-hour pints, dartboard in the back. Duck in out of the Richmond fog. @pigwhistlesf

Eight for when you want the pint and the plate to matter equally: Alembic, Magnolia, Comstock, Bartlett Hall, Sycamore, Southern Pacific, Willows, and Pig and Whistle. Which SF neighborhood still hides your favorite beer-and-a-real-meal spot?

item.title: San Francisco Poke Bowls
item.description: Eight San Francisco poke counters worth the walk-up line, ranked by how fast the fish disappears. Where locals go when the sushi bar wants forty bucks and
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Poke Bowls

Eight San Francisco poke counters worth the walk-up line, ranked by how fast the fish disappears. Where locals go when the sushi bar wants forty bucks and an hour.

Poke Origin — 716 Irving St, San Francisco. The Inner Sunset workhorse near Golden Gate Park, where the line moves fast and the mix-ins stay generous. You point, they build, you leave full for under fifteen bucks. Grab a bowl before you walk the park, not after, when everything good is gone. @thepokeorigin

Fish In The Box — 800 Masonic Ave, San Francisco. This tiny Panhandle spot treats poke like a sashimi counter, bluefin toro and Hokkaido scallop over rice instead of the usual scoop-and-sauce. They close midday to reset, so time it or stand outside reading the hours like the rest of us. Worth the trip up Masonic. @fishinthebox_sf

Happy Poke — 2760 Octavia St, San Francisco. A pocket-sized Cow Hollow counter where you fill out a little clipboard menu and they cut the fish silky, sashimi style. Snag one of the few outdoor tables near Union Street or eat it walking, nobody judges. Closed Mondays, so plan the craving around it. @happypokesf

I'a Poke — 314 Church St, San Francisco. The Mission Dolores standby for a fat sushi burrito or a build-your-own bowl, right where the J-Church spits you out. Counter service, quick turnover, the kind of lunch you eat on the Dolores Park grass ten minutes later. Go before the weekend crowd claims the whole hillside. @iapokesf

Poke Delish — 601 Mission Bay Blvd North, San Francisco. A poke stall parked inside Spark Social, the Mission Bay food yard with fire pits and picnic benches. Traditional Hawaiian bowls with a California hand on the sauce, best eaten out back while somebody's dog steals attention. Closes at five on Sundays, so it's a lunch play. @pokedelish

Poke Bowl — 1250 Ocean Ave, San Francisco. The Ingleside neighborhood pick, a mark-the-sheet build-your-own that stays open till nine thirty when everything else near City College has folded for the night. No frills, big portions, the reliable one when you're out past the tourist map. Parking is easy out here, a small SF miracle. @thepokebowls

Da Poke Man — 24 Willie Mays Plaza, San Francisco. Hawaiian poke slinging out of a truck by Oracle Park, and yes, they set up inside near section 112 on Giants home games. Catch it on a non-game day when the line isn't a hundred orange jerseys deep. Fresh, generous, and cheaper than a ballpark hot dog by a mile. @da_poke_man

Bimi Poke — 135 4th St, San Francisco. Tucked in the Metreon by the AMC, a Hawaiian-Japanese counter doing poke bowls and sushi burritos for the pre-movie crowd. Downtown lunch that won't wreck the afternoon, order the burrito if you want to eat one-handed in a dark theater. Open late enough for the last showtime. @maywen1985

Eight for the poke crawl: Poke Origin and Poke Bowl for fast neighborhood scoops, Fish In The Box and Happy Poke for sashimi-grade cuts, I'a Poke and Poke Delish for the bowl-plus-burrito crowd, Da Poke Man and Bimi Poke for eating on the move. Which SF neighborhood gets your line next?

item.title: San Francisco Burmese Restaurants
item.description: Eight San Francisco Burmese tables worth the Clement Street parking hunt, from a James Beard honored institution to a converted downtown fire house. Tea le
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Burmese Restaurants

Eight San Francisco Burmese tables worth the Clement Street parking hunt, from a James Beard honored institution to a converted downtown fire house. Tea leaf salad is the gateway, then it gets deep.

Burma Superstar — 309 Clement St, San Francisco. The one that put Burmese food on the local map back in 1992, and the line out front still makes the case. Get the tea leaf salad tossed at your table and the samusa soup. They take no reservations, so put your name down and go wander Clement Street until they wave you in. @burmasuperstar

Mandalay — 4348 California St, San Francisco. The oldest Burmese kitchen in the city, open since 1984 and crowned a James Beard America's Classic. The room is unfussy and the regulars hold firm opinions about the sesame beef and the fish noodle soup. Come early, the kitchen keeps its own hours. @mandalayrestaurant_

B Star — 127 Clement St, San Francisco. The little sister up the same Clement strip from Burma Superstar, calmer and easier to walk into on a whim. It roams past Burma into Thai and Chinese comfort food, but the tea leaf salad and coconut rice hold the line. Weekend brunch here is the neighborhood's quiet secret. @bstarbar

Burma Love — 211 Valencia St, San Francisco. Burma Superstar's Mission spinoff, louder and glossier with a full bar for once. Order the pumpkin pork stew, the garlic noodles and a cocktail you cannot get out in the Richmond. Good for the group that argues about where to eat before anyone agrees. @burmalove

Burma Love Downtown — 8 Mint Plaza, San Francisco. The same kitchen tucked into a restored historic fire house off Mint Plaza, a short walk from Union Square. High ceilings, big cocktails and platters built for sharing after a day downtown. Slip in before a show at the nearby theaters. @burmalove

Burmese Kitchen — 3815 Geary Blvd, San Francisco. Once a Tenderloin fixture, it came back from the dead on Geary and the faithful followed west. This is the homestyle end of the spectrum, so go for the mohinga, the pork curry and whatever the specials board is pushing. Quietly one of the best values in the Richmond. @burmesekitchen

Inle Burmese Cuisine — 822 Irving St, San Francisco. Named for the lake back home, it traded Noe Valley for a bigger Inner Sunset room in 2023 and the seats fill fast. The tea leaf salad and mohinga are the tells, and the Thai half of the menu covers your picky friend. Easy stop before or after Golden Gate Park. @inlecuisine

Pagan — 3199 Clement St, San Francisco. Way out at the foggy end of Clement, this Burmese and Thai corner is the name locals drop when they want the flavors without the wait. Ginger salad, tea leaf salad, one good curry, and you will forget the drive out.

Eight for the Burmese map of San Francisco: the 1992 original, the 1984 James Beard classic, two Burma Loves and a foggy Clement sleeper. Which tea leaf salad wins your table?

item.title: San Francisco Indonesian and Malaysian
item.description: Eight San Francisco spots for Indonesian and Malaysian food, a category the city keeps quiet about. Rendang, laksa, sambal, kaya toast, all inside city lim
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Indonesian and Malaysian

Eight San Francisco spots for Indonesian and Malaysian food, a category the city keeps quiet about. Rendang, laksa, sambal, kaya toast, all inside city limits, no bridge toll required. If you figured SF topped out at pho and dim sum, these are the ones worth crossing town for.

Fikscue — 7 Warriors Way, San Francisco. Indonesian spice meets Texas smoke at Thrive City, the rare brisket that tastes of sambal and lemongrass. It made the New York Times best list, then kept the line moving on Warriors nights. Go early on a game day or the good cuts sell out before tip off. @fikscue

Nusa — 3450 Third Street, San Francisco. A Bayview kitchen turning out rendang and nasi campur the way a grandmother in Java would nod at. Chef Jennifer Huang grew up on these flavors and it shows in the depth of every sauce. Catch the Saturday stand at the Ferry Building if Third Street is a trek. @nusa.sf

Rasa Rasa Kitchen — 2200 Bryant Street, San Francisco. The Mission spot known as R2K plates gado gado in a crispy tortilla bowl, which sounds like a gimmick until the peanut sauce wins you over. Beef rendang and soto round out a short, confident menu. Weeknights are calmer if you want a table without the wait. @sf.rasarasakitchen

Warung Nasi Indonesia — 1200 Market Street, San Francisco. A Mid Market counter doing homestyle Indonesian, the kind of nasi and sambal that regulars order without glancing at the menu. Portions lean generous and the heat is honest, so ask where you land before they ladle. Lunch is the sweet spot. @warungnasi.indonesia

Lime Tree Southeast Asian Kitchen — 836 Clement Street, San Francisco. A Richmond mainstay blurring the line between Malaysian, Singaporean, and Indonesian, with a roti canai that has quieted many a debate about who does it best. There is a second kitchen on Irving if the avenues are your side of town. Closed Mondays, plan around it. @limetreekitchensf

Penang Garden — 728 Washington Street, San Francisco. Tucked into Chinatown, a Malaysian and Singaporean menu that surprises anyone expecting another Cantonese room. Order the Hainan chicken or the char kway teow and settle in. It has cooked quietly through decades of the block turning over around it.

M&Y Malaysian Food — 1661 Tennessee Street, San Francisco. A tiny Dogpatch operation built around laksa, wraps, and bowls that travel well if the shipyard fog chases you back to your desk. Bold, colorful plates, portions that earn the trip out here. Weekdays open at noon when the neighborhood is hunting lunch.

Kopiku Indonesian Coffee — 1443 Lombard Street, San Francisco. The city's first Indonesian coffee bar, pulling shots from small Sumatran and Javanese farms and pairing them with kaya toast. Pandan lattes and a pour over worth slowing down for, tucked on a Marina stretch built for drive by. Seating is tight, so time it off peak. @kopikusf

Eight for the Southeast Asian corner SF forgets it has: Fikscue for smoke, Nusa and Rasa Rasa for rendang done right, Warung Nasi for the homestyle plate, Lime Tree for roti, Penang Garden for the Chinatown surprise, M&Y for laksa, Kopiku for the kaya toast finish. Which one are you booking first?

item.title: San Francisco Vegan and Vegetarian
item.description: Eight San Francisco vegan and vegetarian spots that turn skeptics into regulars. The city has been cooking meatless since Greens opened at Fort Mason in 19
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Vegan and Vegetarian

Eight San Francisco vegan and vegetarian spots that turn skeptics into regulars. The city has been cooking meatless since Greens opened at Fort Mason in 1979, and the range now runs from Buddhist temple food to vegan barbecue. Bring the friend who insists they need meat on the plate and watch them go quiet halfway through.

Greens — 2 Marina Blvd, San Francisco. The one that started it all, tucked into a Fort Mason warehouse with the Golden Gate framed in the windows like a postcard nobody staged. Order the mesquite grilled brochettes and grab a window table before the sunset crowd claims them. Weekend brunch is the quiet secret. @greensrestaurant

Shizen — 370 14th Street, San Francisco. Vegan sushi that sounds like a dare and eats like a revelation, ten years deep in the Mission and still packed. The rolls lean on marinated tomato and eggplant where the fish would be, and you stop missing it by the second piece. Go early or brace for the wait. @shizensf

Wildseed — 2000 Union Street, San Francisco. Cow Hollow's airy plant based hangout where the patio does most of the talking on a sunny afternoon. The menu wanders the Mediterranean, the wine list is all vegan, and the crowd skews date night. Split the flatbreads and a carafe, thank yourself later. @wildseedsf

Golden Era — 395 Golden Gate Avenue, San Francisco. A Tenderloin fixture serving Asian comfort food that happens to be entirely vegan, no announcement necessary. The mock meats have converted more carnivores than any pamphlet ever could, and the portions forgive a big appetite. Get the Dragon Phoenix. @goldenerasf

Cha-Ya — 762 Valencia Street, San Francisco. Family run Japanese vegetarian cooking rooted in Buddhist shojin tradition, small room, big flavors, gentle prices. The tempura and the agedashi tofu arrive quiet and confident, the kind of meal that makes vegetables feel like the whole point. Come hungry, leave calm. @chayasanfrancisco

Vegan Mob — 90 Charter Oak Avenue, San Francisco. Toriano Gordon's plant based barbecue landed in the Bayview and the rib tips have a waitlist for a reason. Brisket burritos, garlic noodles, smoked everything, all vegan, none of it apologizing. Bring napkins and low expectations for leftovers. @officialveganmob

Aiso — 4068 18th Street, San Francisco. The Castro newcomer plating vegan tapas that look like they wandered off a fine dining tasting menu. Small sharing plates, a proper cocktail list, and a room that hums on weekends without shouting. Book ahead, order wide, let the table graze. @welcometoaiso

Om Sabor — 370 Grove Street, San Francisco. Cosmic vegan comfort food tucked inside Phonobar in Hayes Valley, hopping across Mexican, Korean, Indian and Venezuelan in one sitting. It started as a pop up and earned a home. That tells you plenty. Pregame the symphony here and skip the tourist traps. @omsabor

Eight for meatless done right: Greens for the view, Shizen for the sushi, Wildseed for the patio, Golden Era for the converts, Cha-Ya for the calm, Vegan Mob for the smoke, Aiso for the date, Om Sabor for the road trip on a plate. Which one wins your Friday?

item.title: San Francisco South Bay Hot Pot
item.description: Eight South Bay hot pot rooms worth skipping the national chains for, from Santa Clara wagyu counters to a Japantown standby, plus two out on the Milpitas
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco South Bay Hot Pot

Eight South Bay hot pot rooms worth skipping the national chains for, from Santa Clara wagyu counters to a Japantown standby, plus two out on the Milpitas and Fremont edge. Cold night, big table, everyone cooks their own. Where the regulars go.

Mikiya Wagyu Shabu House — 3590 Homestead Rd, Santa Clara. The wagyu comes out marbled like a painting and you swish it through the broth about ten seconds before it is done. All you can eat runs three tiers, so the size of the splurge is yours to set. Bring someone who appreciates good beef. @mikiyabayarea

Taichi Pot Shabu Shabu — 2640 Homestead Rd, Santa Clara. Same street as Mikiya, quieter room, individual pots so nobody fights over the spicy side. They handcraft the broths and age the beef, and the after work crowd fills the bar first. Go early or wait. @taichipotshabu

One Pot Shabu Shabu — 19648 Stevens Creek Blvd, Cupertino. Tucked in the Marketplace plaza and running since 2011, back when Cupertino shabu options were thin. Each person gets a pot and a broth, which ends the ordering negotiations. The sesame sauce is why regulars stay loyal. @onepotshabushabu

Revopot — 2934 Aborn Sq, San Jose. The plates ride a conveyor belt past your seat and you grab what looks good. That's either efficient or dangerous depending on your appetite. All you can eat, open late on weekends, easy on the East San Jose crowd. Pace yourself. @revopot_sj

Tasty Pot — 1143 Story Rd Ste 100, San Jose. Taiwanese style, so your pot arrives loaded and you are not building it from an empty broth. They added all you can eat, and the milk tea comes from the same kitchen. A solid weeknight call when you want hot pot without the ceremony. @tastypot.usa

Shabu Time — 171 Jackson St, San Jose. The Japantown pick, individual pots in a room that has fed the neighborhood for years. Certified meats, udon and ramen add ons, and a lunch that moves fast enough for a work break. Walk it off with a loop past the museum after. @shabutimesj

Shabu Shabu Kiwami — 79 S Abbott Ave, Milpitas. The new kid on Abbott, all you can eat with premium cuts and a broth list that rewards the curious. Booths fill on weekends, so put your name down and let the wait build the appetite. Come hungry, leave slow. @shabukiwami

Happiness Hot Pot — 37140 Fremont Blvd, Fremont. Over the Fremont line and worth the drive, a Chongqing room where the beef tallow broth carries real heat. Order the goose intestine if you know it, the house shrimp paste if you are easing in. Bring water and a friend who commits. @happiness_hot_pot2025

Eight for the coldest South Bay nights: Mikiya and Taichi on Homestead, One Pot in Cupertino, Revopot, Tasty Pot and Shabu Time in San Jose, Kiwami in Milpitas, Happiness over in Fremont. Which broth are you starting with?

item.title: San Francisco Marin Burgers
item.description: Eight Marin burgers that locals drive across town for, from a Tiburon dock deck to a Corte Madera park truck. Skip the chains at the mall. Here is the Nort
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Marin Burgers

Eight Marin burgers that locals drive across town for, from a Tiburon dock deck to a Corte Madera park truck. Skip the chains at the mall. Here is the North Bay burger map you keep.

Phyllis' Giant Burgers — 2202 4th St, San Rafael. Four decades in and the line still moves because the griddle never stops. Order the classic with cheese, grab a booth, and let the milkshake carry the conversation. The teriyaki burger sounds wrong and eats right. @phyllisgiantburgers

M&G Burgers — 989 Magnolia Ave, Larkspur. A 1962 counter joint that never chased a trend, and the town loves it for exactly that. Burger, fries, thick shake, no reservation, no fuss. Old-school energy in a downtown that has otherwise gone boutique. @mandg_burgers

Buckeye Roadhouse — 15 Shoreline Hwy, Mill Valley. Open off the 101 since 1937, this is the dressed-up burger with a white-tablecloth backbone. It took Best Burger in the county and did not get quiet about it. Sit at the bar, get the burger and a martini, thank yourself later. @thebuckeyeroadhouse

Sam's Anchor Cafe — 27 Main St, Tiburon. The deck sits right on the water and half the boats tie up to eat. The burger is not reinventing anything. That's the point when the view does the heavy lifting. Ferry over from the city and make a day of it. @sams_cafe

Finnegan's Marin — 877 Grant Ave, Novato. A downtown Irish pub that quietly won Best Burger in Marin and kept the receipt. Open 365 days, patio out back, a pint that arrives cold and correct. The kind of room where the bartender has your order by the third visit. @finnegansmarin

Napa Valley Burger Company — 670 Bridgeway, Sausalito. Gourmet burgers a block off the ferry landing, tourists and locals sharing one patio. Wine-country toppings without the wine-country prices. Grab a window seat and watch the Bridgeway parade go by. @napavalleyburgercompany

Humble Cheeseburger — Town Park at Pixley Ave, Corte Madera. A halal smash-burger truck parked by the post office, and the picnic tables fill fast on a warm Saturday. Crispy edges, potato roll, no attitude. Closed Monday and Tuesday, so plan around it. @humblecheeseburger

Barefoot Cafe — 1900 Sir Francis Drake Blvd, Fairfax. An Italian family cafe hiding a sleeper burger called the Barefoot Special, open from breakfast straight through dinner. Fairfax keeps it funky and this room proves it. Take the patio, order the burger, stay for the ravioli talk. @barefootcafefairfax

Eight for the Marin burger crawl: waterfront decks, a 1962 counter, a park truck, and a pub that keeps winning. Which stop is your Saturday?

item.title: San Francisco Ramen
item.description: Eight San Francisco ramen shops worth the fogged-up windows and the wait, and not one is a mall-food-court chain. The slurp order runs Japantown to the Mis
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Ramen

Eight San Francisco ramen shops worth the fogged-up windows and the wait, and not one is a mall-food-court chain. The slurp order runs Japantown to the Mission to the Marina, tonkotsu to dashi to a beef-bone bowl almost nobody in town makes. Bring a napkin and a little patience. Save this before the next cold night rolls in off the ocean.

Marufuku Ramen — 1581 Webster St, San Francisco. The Japantown mall hides a Hakata tonkotsu so thick and creamy it clings to the hair-thin noodles like a secret. Put your name down, wander the bookstore upstairs, and drift back when they text you. The wait here is a rite of passage, not a warning. @marufukuramenofficial

Nojo Ramen Tavern — 231 Franklin St, San Francisco. The whole point is chicken, a golden paitan so silky it makes pork broth feel loud. Order a few yakitori skewers while you wait and you have built yourself a little Tokyo-alley dinner in Hayes Valley. Dim, cozy, and made for a rainy Tuesday with nowhere to be. @nojoramen

Mensho Tokyo — 672 Geary St, San Francisco. This is the Michelin-listed one, a Tokyo legend's first US shop, and the line out front tells you the rest. The tori paitan is the move, though the lamb bowl has a cult that shows up at opening on purpose. Go early or make peace with standing on Geary a while. @mensho.usa

Taishoken — 665 Valencia St, San Francisco. The Tokyo shop that invented tsukemen back in 1951 planted its flag on Valencia, so order the dipping noodles, not the standard bowl. Cold chewy noodles, a small cup of intense pork-and-fish broth, and you dunk. It feels like a hack the first time and a habit by the second. @taishoken.sf

Izakaya Sozai — 1500 Irving St, San Francisco. A pint-sized Inner Sunset room where the tonkotsu quietly out-punches shops triple its size. Come for the ramen, stay for the yakitori and a cold Sapporo, and book ahead because the locals guard this table. Foggy-night comfort with a wait list attached. @izakayasozaisf

Ushi Taro Ramen — 343 8th St, San Francisco. The rebel of the group runs on beef instead of pork, a rich gyukotsu broth with slices of brisket where the chashu usually sits. If you have slurped every tonkotsu in the city and want a new page, this SoMa spot is your reset button. Small room, loud flavor. @ushi_taro_ramen

Saiwaii Ramen — 2240 Irving St, San Francisco. Deep in the Outer Sunset fog sits a neighborhood workhorse turning out honest tonkotsu and a spicy garlic bowl the regulars order on repeat. No scene, no gimmicks, portions that quietly end your night. The kind of place that makes a gray avenue feel like home. @saiwaiiramen

Hinodeya Ramen — 3340 Steiner St, San Francisco. Family-style dashi ramen near Chestnut, lighter and cleaner than the tonkotsu crowd, built on bonito and kombu instead of pork fat. The wontons and the sudachi bowl are the tells that someone back there cares. Bright, breezy, and kinder on the walk-in wait. @hinodeya_sf

Eight San Francisco ramen bowls, one map: Marufuku (Japantown tonkotsu), Nojo (Hayes Valley chicken paitan), Mensho (Tenderloin, Michelin), Taishoken (Mission tsukemen), Izakaya Sozai (Inner Sunset), Ushi Taro (SoMa beef broth), Saiwaii (Outer Sunset), Hinodeya (Marina dashi). Save it, pick your fog level, go slurp. Which bowl gets your vote?

item.title: San Francisco Persian and Middle Eastern
item.description: Eight San Francisco spots for Persian and Middle Eastern food, one for each night you swear you'll cook and then don't. From North Beach kababs to a Lower
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Persian and Middle Eastern

Eight San Francisco spots for Persian and Middle Eastern food, one for each night you swear you'll cook and then don't. From North Beach kababs to a Lower Haight falafel shaped like a donut, this is the SF crawl worth the parking karma. Save it before your next hummus craving hits.

Maykadeh — 470 Green St, San Francisco. A North Beach fixture since 1983, back when the neighborhood was all red sauce and this was the lone saffron in the room. Come for the lamb, the koobideh off the open flame, and a dining room that still feels like a special occasion. @maykadehrestaurantsf

Lavash — 511 Irving St, San Francisco. Family run in the Inner Sunset, closed Mondays and worth planning your week around. The tahdig comes out crackly and golden, the stews taste like someone's grandmother is checking your plate, and the wine list is built to love Persian food back. @lavashsf

Reem's California — 2901 Mission St, San Francisco. Named for the man'oushe, the Arab flatbread that comes out of the oven blistered and folded warm into your hands. Reem Assil built this Mission bakery as a love letter to Arab street food and California mornings. Order the za'atar, then a second one for the walk. @reemscalifornia

Beit Rima — 138 Church St, San Francisco. Arabic comfort food near Duboce Triangle, the kind of place that turned a whole city onto garlicky chicken and crispy cauliflower. The mujadara is quiet and perfect, the vibe is loud and happy, and the wait is a rite of passage. @beitrima

La Mediterranee — 2210 Fillmore St, San Francisco. Pacific Heights has changed a hundred times since 1979 and this little cafe has not, thank goodness. The chicken pomegranate and the meat cigars run on secret Armenian and Lebanese family recipes. Grab a sidewalk table and watch Fillmore go by. @lamedfillmore

Z Zoul Cafe — 295 Eddy St, San Francisco. The only Sudanese kitchen in the Bay, tucked into the Tenderloin and run like a family reunion. The Emperor Bowl and the shawarma are the move, the prices are a throwback, and the welcome is warmer than the block lets on. @zzoulcafesf

Aicha Moroccan Cuisine — 1303 Polk St, San Francisco. Lower Nob Hill Moroccan built on Fez region recipes, where the tagine arrives under a cone of steam and the couscous is a Friday tradition. Come hungry, stay for mint tea poured from a theatrical height, leave planning a trip to Marrakech.

Palmyra — 700 Haight St, San Francisco. A Lower Haight Syrian counter run by one family, named for an ancient desert city and famous for falafel shaped like a donut. The rotisserie chicken and the hummus with the good olive oil are why regulars keep the line moving. Big platters, small prices.

Eight San Francisco tables, from Persian saffron in North Beach to Syrian falafel in the Lower Haight. Maykadeh, Lavash, Reem's California, Beit Rima, La Mediterranee, Z Zoul, Aicha, Palmyra. Print it, pin it, and start crossing them off. Which SF neighborhood should the next food crawl hit?

item.title: San Francisco Bagels
item.description: Eight bagel shops in San Francisco, and not one of them is the chain by the freeway onramp. The best boil-and-bake in this city hides on side streets from
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Bagels

Eight bagel shops in San Francisco, and not one of them is the chain by the freeway onramp. The best boil-and-bake in this city hides on side streets from NoPa to Bernal, and half the crowd still drives past them for the frozen stuff. Here is where the line is worth it.

Schlok's Bagels & Lox — 1263 Fell St, San Francisco. A takeout window in NoPa where the lox is cured and smoked in house, not pulled from a package. Get there before the sold-out sign goes up around 1:45, because it will. @schloksbagels

Boichik Bagels — 3665 Sacramento St, San Francisco. The Berkeley legend crossed the bridge and Presidio Heights got the payoff: a dense, chewy, Montreal-meets-New-York bagel that sells out most mornings. Open daily until 1:30 or gone. @boichikbagels

Wise Sons Jewish Delicatessen — 3150 24th St, San Francisco. The Mission deli that put SF on the modern Jewish-food map, and the bagels are kettle-boiled with malt syrup the old way. Order one with the pastrami and thank yourself later. @wisesons

The Bagel Bakery — 151 Townsend St, San Francisco. Boiling and brick-oven baking New York style since 1976, tucked near the ballpark in South Beach. It is the quiet old-school pick when everyone else is chasing the new sourdough spots. @the_bagel_bakery

The Laundromat — 3725 Balboa St, San Francisco. Bagels by morning, wood-fired pizza and natural wine by night, all in a converted Outer Richmond laundromat. Come for the everything bagel, stay because nobody wants to leave. @thelaundromatsf

Uncle Benny's Donut & Bagel — 2049 Irving St, San Francisco. The Inner Sunset spot that opens at 4am, so the fog-shift commuters and the after-hours crowd both get theirs warm. Donut in one hand, bagel in the other, no judgment. @unclebennysdonut

Bones Bagels — 741 Diamond St, San Francisco. Naturally leavened sourdough bagels in Noe Valley, crisp outside and tangy enough to eat plain from the bag. Open Thursday through Sunday. That's exactly when the line forms. @bonesbagels

Chicken Dog Bagels — 237 Cortland Ave, San Francisco. A one-man sourdough operation running out of Avedano's butcher shop in Bernal Heights, named after the owner's dog. Saturdays are for walk-up sandwiches, and the line down Cortland tells you it is worth it. @chicken_dog_bagels

The SF eight: Schlok's in NoPa, Boichik in Presidio Heights, Wise Sons in the Mission, The Bagel Bakery in South Beach, The Laundromat in the Richmond, Uncle Benny's in the Sunset, Bones in Noe Valley, Chicken Dog in Bernal. Which neighborhood gets your Sunday morning?

I'm an East Bay agent who eats all over the Bay Area. When you want the East Bay version of any of this, Alameda, Contra Costa, and San Joaquin counties are my home turf.

item.title: San Francisco South Bay Boba and Milk Tea
item.description: Eight South Bay boba stops worth the drive, all independent, zero chains in the mix. If your milk tea loyalty stops at the mall kiosk, this thread is your
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco South Bay Boba and Milk Tea

Eight South Bay boba stops worth the drive, all independent, zero chains in the mix. If your milk tea loyalty stops at the mall kiosk, this thread is your permission slip to wander a little. Save it before the next Friday craving hits.

Pekoe — 3276 S White Rd, San Jose. The split drinks are the move here, half one tea half another in the same cup, so you stop losing the flavor debate with yourself. Open past midnight most nights, which your 11pm sweet tooth will remember fondly. @pekoeteabar

Lacaphe — 740 Story Rd Ste 5, San Jose. A women-owned spot where the Vietnamese coffee does the heavy lifting and the boba tags along happily. Order the ca phe sua da with pearls and you understand why the Story Road line stays long. @lacaphe.sj

Tea Era — 20916 Homestead Rd Ste F, Cupertino. Slinging Taiwanese bubble tea since 2001, back when boba in Cupertino meant one or two places, not one per block. Get the classic milk tea and a side of popcorn chicken, the old-school combo that never needed fixing. @teaeracafe

Boba Oasis — 447 Great Mall Dr, Milpitas. Tucked in the Great Mall for when the outlet-shopping stamina runs out and you need something cold in hand. A tidy little independent counter that quietly outclasses the food-court usual suspects. @thebobaoasis

Boba Pup — 1080 Kiely Blvd, Santa Clara. They pour into collectible glass bottles, so your matcha comes with a keepsake you end up hoarding. Organic tea, real Vietnamese coffee, and a name that earns every dog lover walking past. @bobapupca

MoonTea — 513 S Pastoria Ave, Sunnyvale. Parked on the El Camino corner for a quick pull-off, with teas that lean aromatic and Chinese-tea forward instead of syrup-first. The kind of cup that reminds you tea was the point before the boba boom. @moontea.boba

ChaChaCha — 3623 Thornton Ave, Fremont. A woman-owned corner of Fremont doing pistachio matcha, Nutella milk tea, and croffles for the days one vice will not cover it. Come for the boba, leave planning your return around the 10 Won Ppang. @chachacha_fremont

Milk & Honey Cafe — 34265 Fremont Blvd, Fremont. A family Taiwanese kitchen where the boba shares a menu with hot pot and night-market bites, so the group with mixed cravings all wins. Closed Mondays, so plan the milk tea run for any other day. @milkandhoneyfremont

Eight independent South Bay boba stops, two in San Jose, two in Fremont, one each in Cupertino, Milpitas, Santa Clara, and Sunnyvale. Save this for the next craving and drop the independent shop that belongs on the list. The South Bay bench runs deep.

item.title: San Francisco Fremont Afghan Cuisine, Little Kabul
item.description: Eight stops through Fremont's Little Kabul, the largest Afghan community in the country, most of it packed into a few blocks of Fremont Blvd. Everyone race
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Fremont Afghan Cuisine, Little Kabul

Eight stops through Fremont's Little Kabul, the largest Afghan community in the country, most of it packed into a few blocks of Fremont Blvd. Everyone races to one famous kabob counter and drives past the bakery, the market, and the family spots regulars quietly rotate through. Here is the run, from char-grilled classics to bread that comes out of the oven every few minutes.

De Afghanan Kabob House — 37405 Fremont Blvd, Fremont. The name everyone knows, and the char on the chicken and beef kabob is why. Grab the combo over a bed of rice, tear off some bolani, and understand fast why the line out front keeps moving all afternoon.

DeAfghanan Cuisine — 37395 Fremont Blvd, Fremont. Two doors down from the Kabob House and a separate kitchen after a family split, so locals argue which one wins. Come for the Qabili Palau, lamb buried under rice, raisins, and carrot, and pick your own side.

Maiwand Market — 37235 Fremont Blvd, Fremont. The grocery that anchors the strip, with a bakery firing long slippers of nan afghani through the whole day, plus a halal butcher and shelves of Afghan sweets. This is where the home cooks shop, so time a visit for warm bread.

Afghan Awasana Kabob — 37012 Towers Way, Fremont. Tucked off the main drag, which keeps it a regulars' secret. The draw is the kabob platter and a mantu that people drive across the bay for. Closed Mondays, so plan around it. @afghan_awasana_kabob

Fremont Kabob — 5379 Mowry Ave, Fremont. Off the Blvd near Mowry, open late once the Fremont Blvd spots have shut their kitchens. Order the chopan lamb chops, marinated and charbroiled, with a mound of rice and a side of their green sauce. @fremont.kabob

Authentic Afghan Kebab and Cuisine — 39965 Mission Blvd, Fremont. A newer family kitchen up on Mission that quietly built a following on its Qabuli Palau. Small room, big platters, and staff who steer first-timers toward the right kabob. Closed Wednesdays. @afghankebabandcuisine

Kabob Fusion — 41986 Fremont Blvd, Fremont. Further down the Blvd, where Afghan kabob meets Mediterranean and Turkish on one menu. Handy when the table cannot agree, one person gets the Afghan platter, another a wrap, and the zabiha halal grill covers both. @kabobfusionfremont

Maiwand Village — 5698 Thornton Ave, Newark. One town over, worth the short hop for the sit-down Afghan spread and a room built for big groups. Come with people, order the family-style platters and the aushak dumplings, and settle in. Closed Wednesdays.

That is the Little Kabul run: De Afghanan Kabob House, DeAfghanan Cuisine, Maiwand Market, Afghan Awasana, Fremont Kabob, Authentic Afghan Kebab, Kabob Fusion, and Maiwand Village in Newark. Kabob first or a warm sheet of nan first? Which block are you starting on?

item.title: San Francisco's Excelsior, Mission Street
item.description: Eight stops down one stretch of Mission Street in San Francisco's Excelsior, where the cross streets are named Persia, Russia, Naples and Peru and the food
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco's Excelsior, Mission Street

Eight stops down one stretch of Mission Street in San Francisco's Excelsior, where the cross streets are named Persia, Russia, Naples and Peru and the food follows suit. Most people ride BART past it to the fancier end of the Mission. Their loss. Silver to Geneva, no bridge required.

Excelsior Coffee — 4495 Mission St, San Francisco. Black and Brown owned, flying the flags of Barbados, the Philippines and Mexico over the espresso machine. Come for a cortado, leave with an ube brownie from Ube Area you did not plan on. The corner where the neighborhood wakes up. @excelsiorcoffeesf

Restaurante Familiar — 4499 Mission St, San Francisco. Salvadoran and Mexican under one roof, so the pupusas revueltas and the carne asada plate land on the same table. Cheese-crisped masa, a mound of curtido on top, horchata to wash it down. Family name, family portions.

Recovery Room — 4528 Mission St, San Francisco. A proper neighborhood bar with food, drinks and music all under one sign, open to 2am most nights. A kitchen collab with Hidden Spot EXL means you can eat well past when other kitchens quit. The Excelsior after dark, minus the pretense. @recoveryroomsf

Hong Kong Bakery — 4711 Mission St, San Francisco. A Cantonese buns counter where a dollar or two buys a warm cocktail bun or a BBQ pork bun still fogging its bag. Cash, quick, no frills, gone by mid afternoon on the good days. Regulars grab a pink box and keep walking.

Calabria Bros — 4763 Mission St, San Francisco. The Excelsior still has an old-school Italian deli, and this is it, subs from around 8 dollars on Mission between Russia and Persia. House vinegar and a garlic spread the regulars order extra of. One sandwich feeds you twice if you have any restraint. @calabriabros

El Farolito — 4817 Mission St, San Francisco. The Excelsior outpost of the taqueria that made the Mission-style burrito famous, and the line still moves fast. Super burrito about the length of a forearm, al pastor under ten bucks, salsa bar doing half the work. Cash only, ATM inside. @taquerias_elfarolito

Superstar Restaurant — 4919 Mission St, San Francisco. A Filipino silog counter where 5 to 8 dollars gets you longsilog or tosilog, garlic rice and a fried egg included. Cash only, closed Wednesdays and Sundays, so time it right. The kind of cheap, filling plate the Excelsior runs on.

Mission Comics and Art — 5196 Mission St, San Francisco. The longtime Mission comic shop opened a second store here in 2026, a block past Geneva in a former optometry office, likely the first comic shop the Excelsior has ever had. New releases, back issues and a reason to end the walk indoors. @missioncomics

Eight down Mission Street in the Excelsior: Excelsior Coffee, Restaurante Familiar, Recovery Room, Hong Kong Bakery, Calabria Bros, El Farolito, Superstar, and Mission Comics. Silver to Geneva, no bridge, no BART transfer. Which corner do you start on?
